item.title: Customizing Webhooks
item.description:
Layer5 Cloud calls an HTTP endpoint you choose when three things happen: a person asks for help, a Provider Admin decides a signup request, and a person gains Kanvas access. On a self-hosted deployment you set the three endpoints in Helm. None is set by default, and an unset webhook does nothing. The three names are fixed. Adding a fourth webhook requires a change to Layer5 Cloud itself.

Customize and add your own custom webhook 🔗

Set the chart values. They are written into the server ConfigMap as environment variables. There is no .env file to edit in a Helm install.

item.title: White-labeling (Rebranding)
item.description:
You can change the logo, color scheme, domain name, and other aspects of the user interface to match your own identity. Branding is set per organization. You do not need to self-host to white-label: a hosted organization can use the same theme, logos, links, domain, and mail settings. Self-hosting adds the provider-level defaults that every organization inherits.

Customizing Themes 🔗

The Layer5 Cloud dashboard can be customized with your own branding. An organization sets theme colors and four logos: desktop, mobile, dark desktop, and dark mobile. Theme colors accept only hexadecimal values. Each logo can be at most 500 KB. Layer5 Cloud rejects a color or an oversized logo with an error that names it. The signed-in product, and the sign-in, sign-up, and error pages on the organization’s own domain, use that theme.

item.title: Customizing Layer5 Cloud Deployment with Helm
item.description:
Requirements 🔗

The layer5-cloud chart installs the Layer5 Cloud server and, as subcharts, Kratos and Hydra. The defaults below are those of chart version 0.2.0, which ships with Layer5 Cloud v1.0.278. Run helm show values layer5/layer5-cloud to print the defaults of the version you install. For the install procedure, see Deploying Layer5 Cloud.

Values 🔗

The chart writes env.* values into one ConfigMap and one Secret, and the server pod reads both as environment variables. Sensitive values go to the Secret. Any change to either rolls the server pods.

item.title: Deploying Layer5 Cloud
item.description:
High-level List of Deployment Tasks 🔗

  1. Review the prerequisites for installing Layer5 Cloud on Kubernetes. (docs)
  2. Prepare INIT_CONFIG so the first start creates the provider organization and its Provider Admin. (docs)
  3. Install the layer5-cloud chart. (docs)
  4. Create the OAuth2 client in Hydra. The server does not create it.
  5. Deploy Meshery separately and point it at this deployment as its remote provider. (docs, registration)

Kubernetes-based Installation with Helm 🔗

The layer5-cloud chart is in the Layer5 Helm repository. It deploys the Layer5 Cloud server together with Kratos and Hydra. It does not install PostgreSQL, an ingress controller, or a TLS certificate. Make the decisions in Planning first. The commands below use the release name layer5-cloud in the namespace layer5-cloud.

item.title: Networking
item.description:
Considerations of Peer-to-Peer Communication 🔗

When two people open the same design, their browsers exchange edits directly over WebRTC. Layer5 Cloud takes part only at the start and for presence. Edits do not pass through Layer5 Cloud or Meshery Server.

A self-hosted provider is its own signaling host. Browsers open a WebSocket to /collaboration on your deployment. Users connected to your deployment never signal through Layer5’s hosted service, and there is no public Layer5 signaling server to point them at.

item.title: Identity Services
item.description:
Layer5 Cloud offers a built-in identity provider (IDP), supporting OIDC for normal users and token-based authentication (access, ID, refresh tokens) for API clients with JSON Web Signature (JWS) for token signing. Layer5 Cloud users can sign-up via email and password in addition to social identity providers (Google and GitHub) via OAuth2. See Getting Started with a Layer5 Account for details.

Layer5 Cloud identity services include account recovery, email verification, and social sign-in with Google and GitHub. Password sign-in is on, with a minimum of 8 characters, a check against known-breached passwords, and a rejection when the password is too similar to the account identifier.

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
Layer5 Cloud gives you health endpoints, structured logs with stable error codes, startup messages, and optional OpenTelemetry traces. It does not expose a Prometheus metrics endpoint. Build service-level indicators from your ingress and Kubernetes metrics plus the signals below.

Objectives 🔗

  • Know whether the process is running (/healthz) and whether startup finished (/readyz)
  • Alert on stable error codes, not on message text
  • Turn tracing on only when you have a collector
  • Keep startup logs secret, because provider initialization logs the initial administrator password

item.title: Self-Hosted
item.description:
On-premises Deployment of Layer5 Cloud 🔗

A self-hosted deployment runs the same Layer5 Cloud that Layer5 operates, on infrastructure you control. Your users sign in against your identity services, your organizations and designs live in your database, and Meshery Servers in your network connect to your deployment as their remote provider.

One Helm chart, layer5-cloud, installs the application and its two identity services. You supply the database, the ingress, and the TLS certificate.

item.title: Email / SMTP Troubleshooting
item.description:
Email Debugging Guide for Layer5 Cloud 🔗

This guide explains how to diagnose email sending issues in Layer5 Cloud deployments using the enhanced debug logging and testing features.

Overview 🔗

Email issues in Layer5 Cloud can occur due to various reasons including SMTP configuration problems, template errors, recipient validation issues, or network connectivity problems. This guide provides comprehensive debugging tools and techniques.
